content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new measure of saliency that enables pixel-level explanations for class prediction of images. The Marginal Probability Explanation" estimates the conditional probability of the output given only a single input dimension, integrating out the rest of the features. The measure is computed in practice using the dataset as an estimate to the full sample space. MPE is shown to identify specific pixel-level features that can be adjusted to correctly reclassify misclassified samples. Experiments are evaluated on MNIST and CIFAR-10.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
1) The MPE method seems interesting.
2) The paper is easy to read and follow, not much technical background is necessary to fully understand the paper's proposal and results.

Weaknesses
The paper raises a number of questions and poorly justifies its claims.
1) For Monte Carlo estimation/sampling, why use nonstandard notation like "avg" instead of typical sums and expectations?

2) What if I have very few samples for a given class? What is the sample complexity as a function of dataset size, number of features, assumed convergence of learning, etc.?

3) The classification correction was only tested on the misclassified samples. what happens if you do it on the correctly classified samples? If you automatically applied the method to all samples and all classes, would you only adjust those that were misclassified?

4) Why was different preprocessing used for CIFAR-10 for the two different networks? 

5) Figure 5 is not clear. The "comparison methods" are not described. Why should we compare to random? Why is random a good/sufficient baseline?

6) For the prediction probabilities, why were not all classes shown for Figures 6,7, and 9?

7) The formatting of Figure 7 is very sloppy.

8) "CIFAR" is used generically and not clarified to be CIFAR-10 until the discussion.

9) When the authors say "still make decisions based pixel-level logics" "current CNN structures are not there yet", it's not clear why this is a new observation (why "still"?). As mentioned in related works in the paper, this has been shown to be the case for some time. The authors only evaluate their proposal on a vanilla 4-layer CNN and ResNet-50 rather than something more contemporary. These claims are not justified.

10) Why weren't robust methods evaluated? There are a number of simple methods that have been shown to reduce suspectability to adversarial attacks (regularization, augmentation, etc.). 

11) The claim that saliency maps are not sufficient is not well substantiated, and saliency maps were never compared or evaluated against in any form.

Notes/Other:
1) If MPE can be computed "closed-loop", why not learn with it? Create a regularizer from it, use the batch as the approximation for the whole dataset, learn an "MPE-robust" classifier?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
The paper is generally clear and it is fairly easy to follow what the authors are trying to say.

Quality
The paper makes claims that are unsubstantiated or incorrect based on existing literature. The experiments are insufficient to support the thesis. The method is not sufficiently described or analyzed mathematically. Some formatting is sloppy.

Novelty
The method seems novel, but insufficient experiments do not adequately support the perceived novelty. It is unclear how valuable the method is compared to existing saliency measures.

Reproducibility
The description of MPE is sufficient for implementation. No code is provided, and there is insufficient detail to exactly replicate the experiments.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a potentially interesting idea, but fails to demonstrate its value either mathematically or experimentally.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The work proposes an explanation method "marginal probability explanation" MPE. This method examines the contribution of each input feature (pixel-level contribution). MPE explains the effect of each input dimension by calculating the marginal probability, the paper uses Monte Carlo Sampling to approximate the marginal probability.

For each class, a typical sample from the training dataset is a sample to maximize the marginal probability in every input dimension. It demonstrates the best value selection of each input dimension for each class.

The paper introduced a closed-loop validation process, first, a map is generated using MPE if the sample is misclassified pixels with the lowest MPE are replaced with pixels from the typical sample. The papers show that with very few pixel replacements the image classification changes to the correct label.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- The use of MPE as an explanation is novel.
- Closed-loop validation: My favorite part of the paper, generally it is very difficult to validate the effectiveness of an explanation method. Given the typical sample, the replacement can be done without introducing OOD adversarial effects by masking. It would be interesting to see how this method can be extended to validate other explainability methods like gradient-based methods.
- The section connecting MPE with adversarial attacks is very interesting since it introduces a new way of looking at adversarial attacks. Since typical attacks use the gradient the paper shows with few pixels changes in MPE we can get a very different classification.


Weaknesses:
- Independence assumption: The paper assumes that each input features are independent, although this might be the case for some datasets. This is certainly not a general rule.
- Practicality: To calculate the MPE the paper uses MCMPE the computational cost as mentioned in the paper is  "O(|D|nc), where |D| is the size of the training dataset, n is the dimension of the input, and c is the number of classes. " This is very expensive and unpractical for more realistic datasets like ImageNet which is probably why the paper showed only showed empirical examples on smaller datasets  MNIST and CIFAR.
- Generalizability: It is not clear how MPE can generalize to other domains such as language and time series. Creating an explanation method for one domain limits the overall impact of the work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity--Medium:
The text is easy to follow however the image caption can be improved.
Small suggestions:
Figure 3 -> Maybe explain what a typical sample is here, I know you defined it in the text but just looking at the image one can automatically assume you mean a regular sample from dataset.
Figure 4-> Maybe draw a line separating CNN and ResNet samples.

Quality--Fair:
The method itself is not very practical.

Novelty--High:
Both the explanation method and the evaluation method are quite novel.

Reproducibility--Fair:
No code was provided to reproduce the experiments.
content.summary_of_the_review: I do not think the proposed method is practical and can be used to explain realistic datasets. However, this paper introduces very interesting ideas like closed-loop validation. Also, the experiments are quite creative and I think would be a good metric for interpretability in general like the number of pixels used to correct the classification of different methods although in this case, I am not sure what the typical sample replacement here would be if we use this approach to validate saliency methods for example. The insights about the correlation between MPE and adversarial attacks are very interesting. Also, the use of marginal probability as an explanation is novel. For those reasons, I vote to accept the paper.  I believe future work can use this paper to build a more practical method that uses the ideas proposed here.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes marginal probability explanation, which is an approach to provide pixel level feature importance scores for the outputs black-box classifiers. The approach aims to estimate the marginal probability of each input dimension towards the output, which can be computationally challenging to estimate, so a monte carlo approach is introduced as a way to more easily approximate that probability. The approach is demonstrated on MNIST and CIFAR-10. The MPE approach can also be slightly modified to craft adversarial examples for a model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
- This paper introduces a new method to address an important and challenging problem. 
- The paper demonstrates the MPE method on benchmark datasets with interesting results.
- The idea of a typical sample could actually prove quite useful in conveying the MPE explanation to an end-user. For example, similar to 'counterfactual explanations' the MPE scores can be used to show what minimal perturbation is required to flip a sample's prediction.

### Weaknesses
There are several issues that prevent me from recommending this paper in its current form: 
- The paper does not critically engage with the broader literature and the several past saliency maps that already exist. The paper does not answer the question: why should one use the MPE scores instead of several of the other saliency map approaches that current exist? This question is critical, at this point, for any new method that is proposed in this space. No empirical or theoretical justification is given for the MPE.
- Why the MPE definition? It is unclear to me *why* the marginal probability of a sample should be a good explanation especially given challenges with computational challenges of estimating that marginal probability for high-dimensional inputs?
- A closely related work that this paper should more critically engage with is the paper: "Visualizing deep neural network decisions: prediction difference analysis", which also proposes a similar definition, but approximates it in slightly difference ways. It would be helpful to contrast this work with classes of explanations from the counterfactual explanations category.
- Lastly, the evaluation of the MPE method is unclear or even non-existent in the paper. See the ROAR framework (hooker et. al. 2019) for a simple simulation-based method to evaluate the method. The ROAR framework is similar to what is done in section 4.2.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing in this paper is mostly clear and free of typos. However, this work needs to further engage with the broader literature to specifically highlight the key insights that make the proposed method different from others, and the new capabilities that it provides. As it stands, it is difficult to place this work within the broader context.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper proposes an interesting definition and new approach for saliency maps. However, I am unable to recommend the paper in its current form since several aspects: motivation, evaluation, and contextualization with larger literature is lacking.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a saliency map algorithm based on computing the marginal probability of output upon changing all but one input feature, which estimates the "importance" of that input features. A monte carlo approach is then proposed to compute these marginal probabilities, and a notion of "typical sample" is then defined as the average pixel values that maximizes each class independently. Qualitative experiments are shown to assess the quality of these explanations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**:  The paper is easy to read, and an attempt is made to define saliency maps based on sound characteristics, i.e., upon performing a pixel perturbation.


**Weaknesses**:


**Closely related to SHAP and Prediction Difference Analysis, which are not discussed or compared against**

Closely related methods to the one proposed are SHAP (https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.07874), Shapley sampling (https://shap.readthedocs.io/en/latest/generated/shap.explainers.Sampling.html) and prediction difference analysis (https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.04595). All involve computing marginal probabilities with the same objective of computing feature importance. Regarding their comment "Although shapely valued based explanation is a more comprehensive estimation of the feature significance, the computation cost increases exponentially as the number of feature increases", it is possible have efficient approximations to the shapley value by making the feature independence assumption, which is exactly the approach taken by the original SHAP paper, prediction difference analysis and also implicitly by the proposed approach. Thus the novelty of this paper is minor, especially in light of these approaches.

**(Major flaw) No quantative evaluation, no comparison with other saliency map approaches**

All experiments shown are qualitative in the sense that they do not evaluate the faithfulness (via pixel perturbation test, or remove and retrain test), robustness, or any other metrics of saliency map fidelity, and most importantly, there are no comparisons made with existing saliency methods. Results to "correct" sample classification and perform adversarial perturbations are anecdotal, performed on select data points, as opposed that on the entire dataset. This is a major methodological flaw in this paper.

It is important to note that even gradients (another instance of a saliency map) can also be used to perform misclassifications or "correct" classifications, which indeed corresponds to the canonical methods of adversarial example generation such as the fast gradient sign method (FGSM), and thus it is unclear what advantages the current approach possesses over gradients to generate adversarial examples. There also exist single pixel attacks in the adversarial examples literature (https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.08864), and it is also unclear why one might prefer the proposed approach as opposed to these alternatives.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: This paper is mostly clear, and easy to read, barring the occasional typos.

Quality: The quality of this paper is low, given that no quantitative evaluations or comparisons are performed.

Novelty: As mentioned in the weaknesses section, this paper scores low on novelty due to the existence of highly related methods such as SHAP and prediction difference analysis.

Reproducibility: The method seems easy to reproduce from the description presented in the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents a method that is highly related to existing methods, and performs qualitative experiments without comparisons to any existing methods. Overall, this paper is not ready for publication.

content.title: Marginal Probability Explanation: A Saliency Map with Closed-loop Validation
content.TL;DR: We propose a saliency map using marginal probability for each input dimension whose meaningfulness can be closed-loop validated.
content.abstract: In this work, we propose a saliency map with pixel-level resolution, called Marginal Probability Explanation (MPE), for a black-box classifier. MPE visualizes the contribution of each input dimension to the classifier by calculating marginal probabilities when only one dimension is considered. Marginal probabilities are estimated using Monte Carlo by sampling from the training dataset. Based on MPE, we propose typical samples, i.e. samples that maximize their marginal probability in every input dimension. We verify that our proposed MPE is meaningful through closed-loop validation experiments, where replacing a few pixels with the lowest marginal probability with pixels in the typical sample ``corrects" the classification. Based on experiments, we found deep neural networks are probably still using pixel-level logics for image classification. Moreover, the critical pixels are not necessary related to the subject.
